title: Productivity and Costs, Q2 2026 revised: nonfarm business labor share
measure: Pay of all workers (self-employed pay imputed) as % of nonfarm business output; FRED PRS85006173 is the same series as an index, 2017=100
finding: Fell five quarters running, from 55.3% (Q1 2025) to 52.8% (Q2 2026), the lowest since 1947; the four-quarter average (53.7%) is about 0.9 points below the 2025 average and the lowest since at least 2000.
limits: cannot separate AI; most of the fall came 2001-2010; quarterly s.d. about 0.7 pts; revised; next release 5 Nov 2026

title: Nonfinancial corporations sector: labor share for employees (PRS88003173)
measure: Employee pay as share of nonfinancial corporate output; index 2017=100
finding: Fell from 97.5 (Q1 2025) to 93.3 (Q2 2026), matching the business-sector fall without relying on imputed self-employed pay.
limits: not tied to AI; corporate sector only; revised

title: Shares of gross domestic income: compensation of employees, paid (A4002E1A156NBEA)
measure: Employee compensation as % of US gross domestic income, whole economy
finding: Fell from 53.3% (2019) to 51.5%, 51.4% and 50.9% in 2023-25, the lowest since the mid-1930s; unlike the BLS yearly average, it did fall in 2025.
limits: annual only; not tied to AI; whole economy incl. government; 'lowest since 1930s' read from a summarised listing, check before publishing

title: Shares of gross domestic income: corporate profits with IVA and CCAdj, domestic industries (A445RE1A156NBEA)
measure: Domestic corporate profits as % of US gross domestic income
finding: Jumped from 9.3% (2020) to 11.4% (2021) and has stayed at 11.2-11.4% since, the highest since the mid-1960s; the step came before ChatGPT.
limits: annual; step predates generative AI; profits include all firms, not AI owners

title: Shares of gross domestic income: consumption of fixed capital (A262RE1A156NBEA)
measure: Depreciation as % of US gross domestic income
finding: Flat at 16.3-16.5% since 2021, so faster depreciation does not explain the recent fall in pay's share (a common measurement objection).
limits: annual; measurement check, not a signal

title: Private nonfarm business sector labor share (FRED MPU4910141), as used by the LEAP panel
measure: Labour share of private nonfarm business output, annual productivity-program measure (%)
finding: Reads 58.3% for 2024, about 4 points above the quarterly BLS measure, showing how much the level depends on definition.
limits: value read from LEAP report, not FRED; annual; different scope and method

title: World Employment and Social Outlook: May 2025 update (global labour income share)
measure: Labour income (incl. estimated self-employed) as % of world GDP
finding: Global share 53% (2014) to 52.4% (2024); the Jan 2026 Trends release page gives no new labour share figure.
limits: vintages revised; modelled estimates; not re-read this session

title: Transformation Tracker: capital share indicator
measure: US capital share of factor income (logit), ranked against a simulated 1997-2019 trend distribution; four rating bands
finding: Rates the capital share 'Strong Evidence' of transformation, its top band, while calling it the historical upward trend 'without signs of abatement'; overall verdict 'no decisive evidence of transformation'.
limits: data series not named on page; method paper forthcoming; update schedule not stated

title: Charted: Magnificent 7 market cap as a share of the S&P 500
measure: Seven firms' share of S&P 500 market value (%)
finding: Rose from 9.8% (2014) to 34.6% (2024), with a dip to 21.6% in 2022.
limits: sponsored secondary chart; point in year not stated; mostly pre-ChatGPT rise; valuations not income

title: S&P 500's weight in Mag 7 stocks passes 30% (updated 1 Sep 2026)
measure: Seven firms' share of S&P 500 market value (%)
finding: Says the seven make up about 34% of the S&P 500 and Nvidia about 8%, but gives no as-of date and relies on Visual Capitalist and stock websites.
limits: secondary; undated; cannot fix the stale 2025 gap

title: Exploring the U.S. mega-cap landscape (education paper, Apr 2025)
measure: Cumulative weight of largest 5, 10, 20 S&P 500 constituents, 1970-Feb 2025
latest_value: highest since 1970 (Feb 2025); values only in a chart
finding: The index provider states that the weights of the largest 5, 10 and 20 companies reached their highest points since 1970.
limits: no numbers in text; valuation not income

title: S&P 500: earnings and market cap concentration at record-high levels
measure: Top-10 firms' share of S&P 500 earnings and of market cap, 1990-2025 (Bloomberg data)
finding: Shows the top 10 firms' share of S&P 500 earnings, not only market value, at record highs, which answers the 'it is just a bubble' objection in part.
limits: secondary chart; numbers not extractable; Bloomberg data

title: Trends in AI supercomputers
measure: Share of known AI supercomputer performance owned by industry vs government/academia; by country
finding: Industry's share of AI supercomputer performance in the dataset rose from 40% (2019) to 80% (2025).
limits: dataset covers an estimated 10-20% of global capacity (Mar 2025)

title: How much AI compute do frontier labs use?
measure: Estimated shares of world operational AI compute (H100-equivalents), end 2025
finding: Google owned about a quarter of world AI compute at end 2025, and the five best-resourced developers probably had access to less than half.
limits: tentative estimates; Amazon, Microsoft shares not given

title: AI chip owners (data hub, updated 12 May 2026)
measure: Ownership of leading AI chips/compute by company and customer category (H100e, medians with 5-95% intervals)
finding: The only repeated ownership tracker found; it attributes cloud compute to the cloud firm, not the lab using it.
limits: relies on analyst estimates; 'Other' is a significant minority; excludes smuggled chips in China

title: Follow the CAPEX: Q2 2026 scoreboard
measure: Quarterly capital spending of Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta (US$bn, from company releases)
finding: Four firms spent almost $172bn in Q2 2026 against $155bn in all of 2023; July guidance (Amazon ~$220bn, Alphabet $195-205bn, Meta $130-145bn, Microsoft ~$175bn) sums to $720-745bn.
limits: secondary but quotes releases; finance-lease treatment differs by firm; post's own table says $735-750bn, which does not match its listed guidance

title: Tracking AI's contribution to GDP growth
measure: Contribution of information processing equipment, software, R&D and data-centre construction to real GDP growth (pp, % of growth)
finding: AI-related categories contributed 0.97 points, 39% of real GDP growth, in the first three quarters of 2025, against 28% for the same categories in 2000.
limits: categories not all AI; no import adjustment; blog analysis, not a scheduled series

title: AI investment is booming, but so are imports
measure: AI-related investment as % of GDP and of growth; imports as share of AI investment
latest_value: ~8% of GDP; imports ~35% of AI investment (Oct 2026)
finding: AI-related categories are about 8% of GDP but more than half of real growth over the past year; imports now make up about 35% of AI investment, so much of the spending's income accrues abroad.
limits: asset-manager commentary; definitions not given in text

title: NVIDIA announces financial results for second quarter fiscal 2027
measure: Quarterly revenue, data-centre revenue, GAAP net income (US$)
latest_value: revenue $96.2bn; data centre $89.0bn; net income $59.7bn (quarter to 26 Jul 2026)
finding: Revenue up 106% year on year with a 75% gross margin and about $60bn net income in one quarter, a direct measure of profits flowing to an AI-capital owner.
limits: one firm; company release; profits partly abroad and to global shareholders

title: Union Members 2025
measure: Union members as % of wage and salary workers
finding: Little changed at 10.0% in 2025 (14.7m members), flat near 10% since 2022.
limits: 2025 is an 11-month average (Oct 2025 CPS not collected); proxy for bargaining power

title: Union affiliation by occupation and industry, 2025 (Table 3)
measure: Union members as % of employed, by occupation
latest_value: computer and mathematical 3.7%; management, business, financial 4.3% (2025)
finding: The occupations most exposed to AI are among the least unionised: 3.7% in computer and mathematical jobs against 10.0% overall.
limits: exposure not measured by BLS; 11-month 2025 average

title: Major work stoppages in 2025
measure: Strikes and lockouts of 1,000+ workers beginning in the year; workers involved
finding: 30 major stoppages began in 2025, well above the 2006-2025 average of 17.8, which does not suggest collapsing collective leverage.
limits: large units only; not linked to AI disputes

title: Wage Growth Tracker
measure: Median 12-month wage growth, 3-month moving average, overall/job switchers/job stayers (%)
finding: Switchers' premium over stayers was 1.3 points in Sep 2026, a market-wide proxy for workers' outside options.
limits: not split by AI exposure

title: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, August 2026
measure: Quits as % of employment
finding: Quits were unchanged at 3.1 million (1.9%) in August 2026; low quits signal weak worker leverage.
limits: economy-wide; not tied to AI; no history read this session

title: Negotiating Tech: an inventory of U.S. union contract provisions for the digital age
measure: Technology provisions in union contracts, classified in six sections
finding: Classifies technology clauses from over 175 agreements but gives no counts of AI clauses over time.
limits: not a count series; update schedule unclear

title: Summary of the 2023 WGA MBA
measure: Contract terms on AI
finding: After a strike, writers won terms that 'AI can't write or rewrite literary material' and companies cannot require writers to use AI.
limits: one strongly unionised sector

title: Hollywood studios reach a tentative agreement with writers union
measure: Contract terms on AI
finding: A four-year tentative deal was expected to add rules including 'licensing for AI training'; ratification and final terms not confirmed here.
limits: press report; terms not read at WGA

title: SAG-AFTRA members approve 2025 video game agreement
measure: Contract terms on AI digital replicas; ratification vote
finding: An 11-month strike ended with consent and disclosure rules for AI digital replicas and 15.17% pay increases.
limits: one sector; enforcement unknown

title: ILA members ratify new six-year master contract
measure: Contract terms on automation; wage increase
finding: Dockworkers won a 62% wage rise and 'full protections against automation' to 2030.
limits: automation, not AI specifically; union's own release

title: The simple macroeconomics of AI (NBER w32487)
measure: Task-based estimate of TFP, wage and inequality effects of AI over 10 years
finding: Predicts at most 0.66% (under 0.53% adjusted) TFP gain over 10 years and that AI will 'widen the gap between capital and labor income'.
limits: model; small effects assumed

title: Scenarios for the transition to AGI (NBER w32255)
measure: Wages under automation scenarios
finding: Wages depend on a race between automation and capital accumulation; if full automation is reached 'wages collapse'.
limits: theory; no calibration to current data

title: Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation (JFE 151)
measure: Sales, employment, valuation growth of AI-investing US firms
finding: AI-investing firms grow faster in sales, employment and value, and AI-powered growth 'concentrates among larger firms' with higher industry concentration.
limits: pre-generative AI; employment also rises

cite: Autor, Dorn, Katz, Patterson & Van Reenen 2020
title: The fall of the labor share and the rise of superstar firms (QJE 135(2))
measure: Industry concentration and labour share, US census data
finding: Industries where concentration rose most saw the biggest labour share falls, driven mainly by reallocation to low-labour-share superstar firms.
limits: pre-AI mechanism; AI would need to intensify it

title: The global decline of the labor share (QJE 129(1))
measure: Corporate labour shares across countries
finding: The global labour share has fallen since the early 1980s and cheaper investment goods explain 'roughly half' of the decline.
limits: pre-AI; disputed by later harmonised data

title: Perspectives on the labor share (JEP 38(2))
measure: Labour share trends and causes
finding: As of 2022 the US labour share was at its lowest since the Great Depression and still declining across countries and industries.
limits: review; no AI attribution

title: The elusive explanation for the declining labor share (Annual Review of Economics 14)
measure: Proposed causes of the labour share decline
finding: The literature 'collectively explains the phenomenon many times over', so no single cause, AI included, can be read off the trend.
limits: pre-generative AI

title: Labor share decline and intellectual property products capital (Econometrica 88(6))
measure: Decomposition of the US labour share by capital type
finding: The post-war decline in the measured US labour share is 'entirely explained' by capitalising intellectual property products (software, R&D) in the national accounts.
limits: pre-AI; AI spending is itself largely software/R&D and equipment, so it can lower the measure mechanically

title: Revisiting the global decline of the (non-housing) labor share (AER: Insights 2(3))
measure: Harmonised non-housing corporate labour shares
finding: Harmonised series are stable or rising in all major advanced economies except the US and Canada, casting doubt on technology explanations.
limits: data to late 2010s

title: Has the labour share declined? It depends
measure: OECD labour shares, production vs income perspective
finding: Finds a small decline driven mainly by rising depreciation, and 'little or no decline' on an income (net) basis.
limits: pre-AI; BEA depreciation share flat since 2021

title: Estimating the U.S. labor share (Monthly Labor Review)
measure: Methods for imputing self-employed labour income
finding: The quarterly BLS measure assumes proprietors earn employees' hourly pay; other methods give different levels.
limits: methods note

title: The decline of the U.S. labor share (Brookings Papers on Economic Activity)
measure: US labour share and self-employment imputation
finding: Reported as finding that part of the headline decline reflects how self-employed income is imputed; size not checked this session.
limits: abstract not readable (bot check); detail from memory

title: Tasks, automation, and the rise in US wage inequality (Econometrica 90(5))
measure: Share of wage-structure change due to task displacement
finding: Automation-driven task displacement accounts for 50-70% of changes in the US wage structure over four decades.
limits: pre-AI automation

title: Uneven growth: automation's impact on income and wealth inequality (Econometrica 90(6))
measure: Returns to wealth and inequality under automation
finding: Automation raises inequality 'via returns to wealth', so gains flow to capital owners, not just skilled workers.
limits: theory with calibration; pre-AI

title: Generative AI and firm values (NBER w31222, rev. Jan 2026)
measure: Stock returns by workforce exposure to generative AI
finding: A portfolio long high-exposure, short low-exposure firms earned 5% in the two weeks after ChatGPT; later labour demand and profit patterns fit labour substitution.
limits: market expectations, not realised income

title: More AI-exposed industries and states are benefiting, but results are heterogeneous (ProMarket; SSRN 5375017)
measure: Output, wage bill, employment, labour share by state-industry AI exposure (QCEW 2017-2024)
finding: One s.d. more AI exposure raised output about 10% and cut the labour share about 5 points; workers captured about 29 cents per dollar of AI-driven output growth.
limits: effects start 2021, before ChatGPT; working paper; exposure measure

title: Payrolls to prompts: firm-level evidence on the substitution of labor for AI (arXiv 2602.00139)
measure: Firm spending on online labour marketplaces vs AI providers
finding: Among the most exposed firms, each $1 less spent on online freelancers comes with about $0.03 more AI spending, an order-of-magnitude cost saving.
limits: freelance spending only; spending data provider not checked

title: Generative AI at work (QJE 140(2))
measure: Issues resolved per hour, 5,179 support agents
finding: AI assistance raised productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices; the abstract reports no wage effect.
limits: one firm; productivity, not pay

title: Still waters, rapid currents: early labor market transformation under generative AI (NBER w33777)
measure: Earnings and hours of chatbot adopters, linked surveys and registers
finding: Precise null effects on earnings and hours, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT.
limits: Denmark; early period; also cited at the work stop

title: Applying AI to rebuild middle class jobs (NBER w32140)
measure: Argument on AI and the value of expertise
finding: Argues AI could extend the value of expertise to more workers and help restore middle-skill jobs; 'not a forecast'.
limits: argument, not evidence

title: AI will transform the global economy. Let's make sure it benefits humanity (summarising Cazzaniga et al. SDN 2024/001)
measure: Job exposure; qualitative inequality scenarios
finding: About 40% of global and 60% of advanced-economy jobs are exposed, and 'in most scenarios, AI will likely worsen overall inequality', partly via higher capital returns.
limits: exposure, not outcomes

title: Broadening the gains from generative AI: the role of fiscal policies
measure: Fiscal responses to AI, incl. capital vs labour taxation
finding: IMF note on how tax and spending policy should respond to AI's distributional effects; page could not be read this session.
limits: not read

title: Public finance in the age of AI: a primer (NBER w34873)
measure: Tax base under AI displacement
finding: AI may 'gradually erode' the two main tax bases, labour income and human consumption, pushing towards consumption and other taxes.
limits: theory; links to the influence stop's tax indicator

title: Workers' share of America's income is at a record low before the AI boom even begins
measure: Expert commentary on the Q2 2026 record low
finding: EY's Daco says the productivity gains behind the gap 'largely predate the AI boom' but 'I don't think there's a floor'.
limits: news; 14.9% profit-margin figure unsourced

title: U.S. workers' share of national income falls to a new low
measure: Expert commentary on the Q1 2026 low
finding: JPMorgan's Feroli sees a 'level shift before and after the pandemic' in returns to capital, not an AI effect; reported Q1 2026 at 53.7% (current vintage about 53.6%).
limits: news; shows revision between vintages

title: Forecasting the economic effects of AI (NBER w35046)
measure: Median forecasts of US labour share, by group and AI-progress scenario (%)
finding: Economists expect 54.3% in 2030 and 50.0% in 2050 (45.0% if AI progress is rapid); AI experts expect 40.0% in the rapid 2050 case.
limits: medians only; definition differs from BLS quarterly series

title: LEAP wave 7 report
measure: Median forecasts of private nonfarm labour share (FRED MPU4910141), experts/superforecasters/public
finding: All three groups expect 58% in 2026 and 56% in 2030; for 2040 experts say 51%, superforecasters and public 53%.
limits: unconditional, not AI-specific; surveyed Mar 2026

title: Econ Scenario Explorer v1.0
measure: Modelled US labour and capital shares in 2030 under three AI scenarios
finding: Labour share 59.4% (modest), 56.1% (substantial) or 45.2% (extreme AI) in 2030, from about 60% today.
limits: AI-firm model; 'today' baseline differs from BLS

title: Labor Automation Forecasting Hub
measure: Community forecasts of US labour share of national income
finding: Forecasters put the labour share at 58.3% in 2030 and 55.6% in 2035 on an unconfirmed series.
limits: series and baseline not confirmed; not re-read this session

title: AI 2040
measure: US wage bill as share of economy
finding: A normative 'Plan A' scenario has the wage bill falling to about 10% of the economy by 2033-35.
limits: scenario, not best guess; not re-read this session

title: Global economic and financial implications of AI: lessons from a scenario-planning exercise (IMF Note 2026/002)
measure: Scenario framework for AI's macro-fiscal effects
finding: Says capital owners 'capture a large share of the gains' and recommends fiscal analysis include scenarios with persistent labour-share declines; gives no estimate.
limits: qualitative
